why_how.text: Stop and yield signs share red and white, but they look different and ask for different things.
A stop sign also comes with a set order for where to stop, starting with the stop line.

scenario.text: Dev approaches a red eight-sided sign with white letters, and the stop line is painted a little past the sign.

reasoning.text: An eight-sided red sign with white letters is a stop sign, and the stop line comes first in the stopping order even when it is beyond the sign.

result.text: Dev makes a full stop at the stop line and waits until crossing traffic and pedestrians have cleared.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a yield sign like a stop sign, or a stop sign like a yield sign, because both are red and white.

correction.text: A stop sign demands a full stop every time; a yield sign demands slowing and giving way to traffic already in the intersection or on the road you are entering.

memory_support.text: Octagon stops you; triangle slows you.

prompt.text: Carmen reaches a stop sign at a corner with no stop line, but a crosswalk is painted across her road. Where does she stop?

answer.text: At the crosswalk, because with no stop line the crosswalk comes next in the stopping order.

rationale.text: The order is the stop line first, then the crosswalk if there is no line, and otherwise just before entering the intersection.

narration.text: This lesson covers two of the most important regulatory signs you will meet: the stop sign and the yield sign. A stop sign is an eight-sided red sign with white letters. A yield sign is a red and white triangle with red letters. They share colors, but they ask for very different things. A stop sign requires a full stop and a wait until crossing traffic and pedestrians have cleared. A yield sign means slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic in the intersection or on the road you are joining. After the two signs, we will work through exactly where your vehicle should come to rest at a stop sign.

lines.text: Stop line, even beyond the sign.

narration.text: Start with the stop sign. It is an eight-sided red sign with white letters. When you reach one, you must come to a full stop. Slowing down and rolling on does not meet that rule. After stopping, you wait until crossing traffic and pedestrians have cleared before you move. That wait is part of the rule, not an extra courtesy. If there is a stop line, that is where you stop, even if the line is painted beyond the sign. Without a line, you stop near the edge of the intersection, look both ways and go when it is safe. So the stop sign always asks for the same two things: a full stop, and a wait until the way is clear.

Now the yield sign. It is a red and white triangle with red letters. Compare that with the stop sign, which is red with white letters and has eight sides. The colors overlap, so the shape and the letter color are what tell them apart: eight sides with white letters means stop, and a triangle with red letters means yield. A yield sign means slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic in the intersection or on the road you are joining. The key idea is giving way. Traffic already in the intersection, or already on the road you are entering, goes first, and you fit in behind it once you have slowed and the way is clear.

lines.text: Stop sign: full stop every time.
Yield sign: slow and give way.

narration.text: Here is a common trap. Because both signs are red and white, it is easy to mix up what each one asks. A stop sign demands a full stop every time, even when the road looks empty. A yield sign demands slowing and giving way to traffic already in the intersection or on the road you are entering. Questions often describe the sign rather than naming it. If the description says eight sides, red, with white letters, it is a stop sign, and the answer involves a full stop. If it says a red and white triangle with red letters, it is a yield sign, and the answer involves slowing and giving the right-of-way.

Here is a quick check: Carmen reaches a stop sign at a corner. There is no stop line painted on her road, but there is a crosswalk. Where should she bring her car to a full stop? Work it out before reading on. The answer is at the crosswalk. The stopping point order is the stop line first, then the crosswalk if there is no line, and otherwise just before entering the intersection. Because there is no line here, the crosswalk is next in that order. If there were a stop line, she would stop at that line, even if it were painted beyond the sign. With neither, she would stop just before entering the intersection.

To close, put the pieces together. The stop sign is an eight-sided red sign with white letters, and it requires a full stop and a wait until crossing traffic and pedestrians have cleared. The yield sign is a red and white triangle with red letters, and it means slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic in the intersection or on the road you are joining. At a stop sign, choose your stopping point in order: the stop line first, then the crosswalk if there is no line, and otherwise just before entering the intersection. Next we turn to signs that tell you whether you may enter a road at all, and which way each lane may go.

why_how.text: Some signs tell you that you may not drive into a road, and one tells you that you already have.
Other signs tell you which way each lane may go and which side of an obstruction to pass.

scenario.text: Priya sees a Do Not Enter sign at the opening of a street she meant to turn into.

reasoning.text: A Do Not Enter sign at a road opening means she may not drive into that road, unlike a Wrong Way sign, which would mean she was already in an oncoming lane.

result.text: Priya does not turn in and finds another way.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking Wrong Way and Do Not Enter mean the same thing.

correction.text: A Wrong Way sign means you are already in an oncoming lane, while a Do Not Enter sign at a road opening warns you not to go in at all.

memory_support.text: Do Not Enter keeps you out; Wrong Way turns you around.

prompt.text: Nate leaves a parking lot, turns onto a road and then sees a Wrong Way sign facing him. What has happened, and what comes next?

answer.text: He has turned into a lane of oncoming traffic, so he should pull off, turn around and go back as quickly and safely as he can.

rationale.text: A Wrong Way sign means you are already in an oncoming lane; a Do Not Enter sign is the one that warns you before you go in.

lines.text: Wrong Way and Do Not Enter.

narration.text: This lesson covers the signs that control where you may drive. Two of them are easy to confuse. A Wrong Way sign means you turned into a lane of oncoming traffic. A Do Not Enter sign at a road opening means you may not drive into that road at all. Alongside them is the One Way sign, which means traffic on that road moves in a single direction. We will also look at lane control signs, posted beside or above the road, which use arrows to show which way each lane may go, and the Keep Right sign, which means traffic must pass only on the right side of a feature or obstruction.

lines.text: You are in an oncoming lane.

narration.text: A Wrong Way sign tells you that a mistake has already happened. It means you turned into a lane of oncoming traffic. The guide's instruction comes in three steps: pull off, turn around and go back. It adds how to do it: as quickly and safely as you can. The guide asks for both together, quick and safe. Compare this with a Do Not Enter sign, which you see at a road opening before you go in. The Wrong Way sign is different because by the time you see it, you are already in an oncoming lane. So the answer to a Wrong Way sign is not to keep going. Pull off, turn around and go back as quickly and safely as you can.

A Do Not Enter sign stands at a road opening, and it means you may not drive into that road. Unlike the Wrong Way sign, it reaches you before the mistake, so the correct response is simply not to turn in. The One Way sign is the second half of this pair. It means traffic on that road moves in a single direction. Read the two signs as answers to different questions. Do Not Enter answers whether you may drive into this road from here, and the answer is no. One Way answers which way traffic on the road moves, and the answer is a single direction. Neither sign tells you to turn around; that is the Wrong Way sign's job.

lines.text: Wrong Way: already in an oncoming lane.
Do Not Enter: do not go in.
Ask: before or after the turn?

narration.text: Here is a trap many learners fall into. Wrong Way and Do Not Enter sound alike, and both deal with going the wrong direction, so it is tempting to treat them as one sign. They are not. A Wrong Way sign means you are already in an oncoming lane. A Do Not Enter sign at a road opening warns you not to go in at all. A simple test helps. Ask whether the driver is still outside the road or already in it. If the driver is at the opening, the Do Not Enter sign applies, and the answer is not to drive in. If the driver has already turned into an oncoming lane, the Wrong Way sign applies: pull off, turn around and go back.

lines.text: Posted beside or above the road.
Keep Right: pass only on the right.

narration.text: Two more signs manage how you move within the road. Lane control signs are posted beside or above the road, and they use arrows to show which way each lane may go. Read the arrow over or beside your lane, and you know which directions that lane allows. The Keep Right sign has a different job. It means traffic must pass only on the right side of a feature or obstruction. Notice the word only: passing on the left side of that feature or obstruction is not allowed. So lane control arrows answer which way each lane may go, while the Keep Right sign answers which side of a feature or obstruction you pass on, and the answer is the right side.

lines.text: A Wrong Way sign faces him.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Nate leaves a parking lot and turns onto a road. A moment later he sees a Wrong Way sign facing him. What has happened, and what should he do next? Work it out before reading on. Nate has turned into a lane of oncoming traffic. The guide says to pull off, turn around and go back as quickly and safely as he can. This is not a Do Not Enter situation. A Do Not Enter sign at a road opening warns a driver not to go in at all, before the turn. A Wrong Way sign means the driver is already in an oncoming lane, which is exactly where Nate is now. So he pulls off, turns around and goes back.

lines.text: Arrows and Keep Right guide lanes.

narration.text: To close, line up the signs from this lesson. A Wrong Way sign means you turned into a lane of oncoming traffic, so pull off, turn around and go back as quickly and safely as you can. A Do Not Enter sign at a road opening means you may not drive into that road. A One Way sign means traffic on that road moves in a single direction. Lane control signs, beside or above the road, use arrows to show which way each lane may go. And a Keep Right sign means traffic must pass only on the right side of a feature or obstruction. Next we move from where you may drive to how fast, starting with what a speed limit sign really means.

why_how.text: A speed limit sign sets a maximum, and conditions can require you to go slower than it.
Missouri also has default limits, an interstate minimum, and a commission that can adjust the uniform maximums.

scenario.text: Omar is about to enter an interstate in normal conditions but feels nervous and plans to drive about twenty-five miles per hour.

reasoning.text: Under normal conditions you may not drive slower than forty miles per hour on an interstate, and twenty-five miles per hour is the town default, not an interstate speed.

result.text: If forty miles per hour is too fast for him, Omar should use another route.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing the posted speed limit is always a safe speed to drive.

correction.text: A speed limit sign shows the legal maximum under ideal conditions, and the law requires you to slow down when hills, curves, slick roads, short sight lines, pedestrians, cyclists or slow vehicles make that speed unsafe.

prompt.text: Omar feels nervous at highway speed and plans to drive about twenty-five miles per hour on an interstate in normal conditions. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. Under normal conditions he may not drive slower than forty miles per hour on an interstate, so if that is too fast for him he should use another route.

rationale.text: Twenty-five miles per hour is the default inside cities, towns and villages, while forty miles per hour is the floor for normal interstate driving.

narration.text: This lesson is about speed limits in Missouri. We start with what a speed limit sign actually tells you: the legal maximum under ideal conditions. Then we look at the defaults the guide lists for roads where no other limit is posted, beginning with the twenty-five miles per hour limit inside a city, town or village. Interstates add something many drivers forget, a minimum speed, and under normal conditions you may not drive slower than forty miles per hour on one. Finally, we will see the default maximums for different road types and the body that can set limits above or below them, the Missouri Highway and Transportation Commission.

lines.text: Slow for hills, curves, slick roads.
Slow for short sight lines too.

narration.text: A speed limit sign shows the legal maximum under ideal conditions. Ideal is the important word. The guide says the law requires you to slow down when conditions make the posted speed unsafe, and it lists them: hills, curves, slick roads, short sight lines, pedestrians, cyclists or slow vehicles. Any one of them can be enough. A slick curve, a hill that shortens your sight line, or a cyclist ahead can each make the posted number too fast. So the sign does not promise that its speed is safe right now. It tells you the most you may drive when everything is ideal, and the law expects you to go slower when it is not.

lines.text: Unposted city, town or village: twenty-five.
Interstate minimum: forty in normal conditions.
Too fast for you? Use another route.

narration.text: Two numbers come up again and again. Inside a city, town or village, the speed limit is twenty-five miles per hour whenever no other limit is posted. That default fills the gap when you see no sign at all. Interstates work differently, because they also have minimum speeds. Under normal conditions you may not drive slower than forty miles per hour on an interstate. The guide is practical about drivers who find that uncomfortable: if forty miles per hour is too fast for you, use another route. So one number is a default maximum for unposted town streets, and the other is a floor that keeps interstate traffic from moving too slowly in normal conditions.

Here is a trap that catches many learners. Both of these numbers are low, so they are easy to swap. The twenty-five miles per hour default applies inside cities, towns and villages, while forty miles per hour is the floor for normal interstate driving. One is a ceiling and the other is a floor. If a question describes an unposted street in a town and asks the limit, the answer is twenty-five miles per hour. If it describes an interstate in normal conditions and asks how slowly you may go, the answer is forty miles per hour. When you read the question, first ask what kind of road it is, then ask whether it wants a maximum or a minimum.

lines.text: Other roads outside urbanized areas: sixty.

narration.text: The guide also lists default maximum speeds by road type. For rural expressways, the default maximum is sixty-five miles per hour. The default maximum is sixty miles per hour in two quite different places: on interstates, freeways and expressways inside urbanized areas, and on other roads outside urbanized areas. Lettered roads have a default maximum speed of fifty-five miles per hour. Notice how the sixty default groups together roads that seem unrelated, a busy urban interstate and a road outside an urbanized area. Learn that pairing as a unit. Then the two remaining numbers are easy to place: sixty-five belongs to rural expressways, and fifty-five belongs to lettered roads.

lines.text: Commission may raise or lower limits.

narration.text: Defaults are not the final word. The Missouri Highway and Transportation Commission may set limits above or below the uniform maximums for safety or to keep traffic moving. So a posted limit can differ from the default in either direction. The guide gives an example of where lower limits show up. It says Missouri has more than one thousand three hundred miles of interstate highway, and lower limits are often posted on urban interstates where interchanges and merging traffic are frequent. So even though the default for interstates inside urbanized areas is sixty miles per hour, you will often see a lower number posted where interchanges and merging traffic are frequent.

lines.text: Omar is nervous at highway speed.
He plans twenty-five on an interstate.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Omar is nervous at highway speed. He is about to enter an interstate in normal conditions and plans to drive at about twenty-five miles per hour to feel safe. Is that allowed, and what does the guide suggest? Work it out before reading on. It is not allowed. Under normal conditions you may not drive slower than forty miles per hour on an interstate. Twenty-five miles per hour is the default limit inside cities, towns and villages, not an interstate speed. The guide's advice for drivers like Omar is clear: if forty miles per hour is too fast for you, use another route instead of the interstate.

lines.text: Twenty-five in town, forty interstate floor.
Sixty-five, sixty, fifty-five by road type.

narration.text: To close, here is the whole picture. A speed limit sign shows the legal maximum under ideal conditions, and the law requires you to slow down when conditions make that speed unsafe. Inside a city, town or village, the limit is twenty-five miles per hour when no other limit is posted, and the interstate floor is forty miles per hour under normal conditions. The defaults are sixty-five for rural expressways, sixty for urbanized interstates, freeways and expressways and for other roads outside urbanized areas, and fifty-five for lettered roads, and the Missouri Highway and Transportation Commission may set limits above or below those uniform maximums.

why_how.text: Railroad crossings use a set of signs and signals, and each one carries a different duty.
Then come the rules for where to stop, the gate, racing trains, shifting gears and second trains.

scenario.text: Grace reaches a crossing where red lights are flashing and the gate is coming down.

reasoning.text: Alternately flashing red lights or a lowering gate mean she must stop and stay stopped, between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest track.

result.text: Grace stops in that range, never drives around the gate, and waits until the train has passed.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a crossing with flashing lights the same as a crossbuck alone, and just yielding.

correction.text: A crossbuck by itself carries a yield duty, while alternately flashing red lights or a lowered gate carry a duty to stop and wait for the train.

memory_support.text: Round warns, X yields, lights stop.

prompt.text: Grace is stopped at a lowered gate with flashing red lights. A train passes, the lights keep flashing, and there are two tracks. What should she do?

answer.text: Stay stopped, never drive around the gate, and check for a second train before crossing, since lights may keep flashing after a train clears.

rationale.text: Flashing red lights or a lowered gate carry a duty to stop and stay stopped until the train has passed, and where there are two or more tracks you check for a second train before crossing.

lines.text: Lights or a gate mean stop.

narration.text: This lesson covers railroad crossings, where the signs and signals come in a set order and each carries a different duty. First, a round advance warning sign, and in some places a pavement marking, tells you a railroad crossing is ahead. At the crossing itself stands the white X-shaped crossbuck, which means the same as a yield sign, so you must yield to trains. Some crossings add alternately flashing red lights or a lowering gate, and there you must stop and stay stopped until the train has passed. We will also cover where to stop, why you never race a train, why you avoid shifting gears on the tracks, and the second-train check.

lines.text: Some places add a pavement marking.
Crossbuck: a white X at the crossing.
A sign beneath gives the track count.

narration.text: The first warning is the round advance warning sign, and in some places a pavement marking, telling you a railroad crossing is ahead. Its round shape sets it apart from the X-shaped crossbuck placed at the crossing itself. So the round sign comes first, while you still have room to prepare, and the crossbuck marks the tracks. The white X-shaped crossbuck means the same as a yield sign, so you must yield to trains. A sign beneath the crossbuck gives the number of tracks, which matters later, because where there are two or more tracks you must check for a second train. Remember the order: round sign ahead, then the X at the crossing.

lines.text: Flashing red lights or a gate: stop.
Stay stopped until the train passes.
Fifteen to fifty feet from the track.

narration.text: Some crossings have more than a crossbuck. Where a crossing has alternately flashing red lights or a lowering gate, you must stop and stay stopped until the train has passed. The guide also tells you where to stop. When the red lights flash or the gate is down, stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest track. The distance is measured from the nearest track, so on a crossing with several tracks, use the closest one. And one rule has no exceptions: never drive around the gate. A lowered gate is not an obstacle to work around. It is the signal to stop and stay stopped until the train has gone by.

lines.text: Flashing lights or lowered gate: stop.

narration.text: Here is a trap that appears often. A crossbuck by itself carries a yield duty, while alternately flashing red lights or a lowered gate carry a duty to stop and wait for the train. Many learners pick one answer for every crossing. Some think every crossing requires a full stop, and others think the crossbuck alone lets them roll through without looking. Neither is right. At a crossbuck with no lights or gate, you yield to trains, the same as at a yield sign. Once the red lights are flashing or the gate is down, the duty becomes a stop, and you stay stopped until the train has passed. Read the question for lights and gates before you answer.

lines.text: Room for your whole vehicle first.
Do not shift gears on the tracks.
Lights may flash after a train.

narration.text: Three habits keep you safe on the tracks themselves. First, never race a train to a crossing. Second, never start across the tracks until there is room for your whole vehicle on the far side, so no part of your vehicle is left on the tracks. Third, avoid shifting gears while crossing railroad tracks, in case the vehicle stalls. Then there is the second-train rule. Crossing lights may keep flashing after a train clears, and where there are two or more tracks, check for a second train before crossing. That is why the sign beneath the crossbuck that gives the number of tracks is worth reading as you approach.

lines.text: Grace waits at a lowered gate.
A train passes; lights keep flashing.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Grace has stopped at a crossing where the red lights are flashing and the gate is down. A train passes, but the lights keep flashing, and the sign beneath the crossbuck shows two tracks. What should Grace do? Work it out before reading on. She stays stopped and never drives around the gate. Crossing lights may keep flashing after a train clears, and where there are two or more tracks, she must check for a second train before crossing. Flashing red lights or a lowered gate carry a duty to stop and stay stopped until the train has passed, and she does not start across until there is room for her whole vehicle on the far side.

lines.text: Crossbuck yields; lights or gate stop.

narration.text: To close, follow a crossing from start to finish. A round advance warning sign, and in some places a pavement marking, tells you a crossing is ahead. At the crossing, the white X-shaped crossbuck means yield to trains, and a sign beneath it gives the number of tracks. Alternately flashing red lights or a lowering gate mean stop and stay stopped until the train has passed, between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest track, and never drive around the gate. Never race a train, never start across without room for your whole vehicle on the far side, avoid shifting gears on the tracks, and check for a second train where there are two or more tracks.

why_how.text: Work zone signs warn that work is going on on the roadway or beside it, so they call for extreme care.
The guide sets conduct rules for any work zone and minimum fines for speeding or passing on Missouri state roads.

scenario.text: Leo sees a fluorescent orange Road Work Ahead sign on a Missouri state road and wants to pass a slow car.

reasoning.text: Orange signs mean work is going on, so he must stay alert, obey the signs and remember the minimum fines for speeding or passing in a work zone.

result.text: Leo stays behind the slow car, avoids distractions and watches for workers and vehicles moving in and out.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating orange work zone signs as advice that matters only when workers are in sight.

correction.text: Be extremely careful whenever work zone signs appear, because some kind of work is going on on the roadway or beside it.

memory_support.text: Orange means work: alert and obey.

prompt.text: Leo is on a Missouri state road past a Road Work Ahead sign and thinks about passing a slow car inside the work zone. What should he keep in mind?

answer.text: A driver caught speeding or passing in a work zone faces a minimum fine of two hundred fifty dollars the first time, so he should stay alert, avoid distractions and obey the signs.

rationale.text: In any work zone, stay alert for lower speed limits, narrow lanes and workers, avoid distractions, obey the signs and watch for vehicles moving in and out.

narration.text: This lesson and the next one cover work zones. Work zone signs are fluorescent orange, and flaggers or other devices may guide you through the work area. The guide asks you to be extremely careful whenever work zone signs appear, because some kind of work is going on on the roadway or beside it. Missouri roads have several kinds of work zones, and knowing them helps you predict what you will meet as you drive through. In this lesson we look at the signs, the conduct the guide expects in any work zone, and the minimum fines for speeding or passing in a work zone on Missouri state roads. The next lesson walks through the zone types.

lines.text: Flaggers or devices may guide you.
Loose Gravel, Right Lane Closed Ahead.

narration.text: Color is your first clue. Work zone signs are fluorescent orange, which makes them easy to pick out from the signs around them. Inside the work area, flaggers or other devices may guide you through. The words on the signs tell you what kind of work to expect. Common work zone signs include Road Work Ahead, Fresh Oil, Loose Gravel and Right Lane Closed Ahead. Each one names something you are about to meet: road work, fresh oil on the surface, loose gravel, or a right lane that is closed ahead. When an orange sign appears, read its words, get ready for what it describes, and follow any flagger or device guiding you through the work area.

lines.text: Stay alert: lower limits, narrow lanes, workers.
Watch vehicles moving in and out.

narration.text: Once you are in a work zone, the guide gives a clear list. In any work zone, stay alert for lower speed limits, narrow lanes and workers. Avoid distractions. Obey the signs. And watch for vehicles moving in and out. Each item matches something that can change inside a work zone. The speed limit may be lower than on the road outside it. The lanes may be narrower, leaving less room around you. Workers may be near traffic. And work vehicles may enter or leave the travel lanes. That is why the guide says to be extremely careful whenever work zone signs appear: some kind of work is going on on the roadway or beside it.

lines.text: Orange signs are not mere advice.
Speeding or passing brings minimum fines.

narration.text: Here is a common mistake: treating orange signs as friendly advice that only matters when workers are in sight. The guide disagrees. Be extremely careful whenever work zone signs appear, because some kind of work is going on on the roadway or beside it. And the law backs that up. On Missouri state roads, a driver caught speeding or passing in a work zone faces a minimum fine of two hundred fifty dollars the first time and three hundred dollars for each repeat, plus any other lawful fines. Notice that the fine covers passing as well as speeding, and that these amounts are minimums. Other lawful fines can be added on top of them.

title.text: Check: passing in a work zone

lines.text: He wants to pass a slow car.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Leo is driving on a Missouri state road and sees a Road Work Ahead sign. He is running late, and a slow car is ahead of him inside the work zone. He thinks about passing it. What should Leo keep in mind? Work it out before reading on. A driver caught speeding or passing in a work zone on Missouri state roads faces a minimum fine of two hundred fifty dollars the first time and three hundred dollars for each repeat, plus any other lawful fines. Beyond the fine, the guide's conduct rules apply: stay alert for lower speed limits, narrow lanes and workers, avoid distractions, obey the signs and watch for vehicles moving in and out.

lines.text: Orange signs: work on or beside the road.
Minimum fines for speeding or passing.

narration.text: To close, gather the work zone basics. Work zone signs are fluorescent orange, flaggers or other devices may guide you, and common signs include Road Work Ahead, Fresh Oil, Loose Gravel and Right Lane Closed Ahead. Whenever they appear, be extremely careful, because work is going on on the roadway or beside it. In any work zone, stay alert for lower speed limits, narrow lanes and workers, avoid distractions, obey the signs and watch for vehicles moving in and out. Speeding or passing in a work zone on Missouri state roads brings minimum fines. Missouri roads have several kinds of work zones, and the next lesson shows each one so you can predict what you will meet.

why_how.text: Each kind of work zone asks something different of you, so recognizing the type tells you what to do.
Two pairs are easy to mix up: shoulder work versus lane closures, and flagging operations versus mobile work zones.

scenario.text: Ivy sees a protective vehicle in her lane with a flashing arrow panel and a Slow Vehicles sign, with work vehicles ahead.

reasoning.text: That is a mobile work zone: slow or stopped work vehicles move along a travel lane, and the arrow panel shows which lane to merge into.

result.text: Ivy follows the arrow panel's direction, merges, and watches for several slow or stopped work vehicles and for workers stepping out.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every work zone just means slowing down.

correction.text: A shoulder work zone asks you mainly to slow down, while a lane closure also asks you to merge into an open lane and drop to the work zone speed limit.

memory_support.text: Shoulder: slow. Closure: merge. Flaggers: be ready to stop. Mobile: follow the arrow.

prompt.text: Ivy comes over a rise and finds a slow truck with a flashing arrow panel and a Slow Vehicles sign, with work vehicles moving ahead. What kind of zone is this, and what should she do?

answer.text: It is a mobile work zone, so she follows the direction on the flashing arrow panel, merges into the lane it shows and watches for several slow or stopped work vehicles.

rationale.text: A mobile work zone moves along a travel lane behind a protective vehicle with an arrow panel, unlike a flagging operation, a fixed site with flaggers at both ends.

narration.text: In the last lesson you saw that Missouri roads have several kinds of work zones. Now we meet them one at a time. A shoulder work zone is one where the work is on or past the shoulder. A lane closure shuts a lane, and you merge into the marked open lane. A flagging operation closes one lane of a two-lane, two-way road, with flaggers at each end. And a mobile work zone moves: slow or stopped work vehicles move along a travel lane, and workers may step out. Each type asks something a little different of you, from simply reducing speed to merging, stopping for flaggers, or following a flashing arrow panel.

lines.text: Shoulder work: on or past the shoulder.
Lane closure: merge into the open lane.
Slow to the work zone limit.

narration.text: Start with the two simplest types. For a shoulder work zone, where the work is on or past the shoulder, reduce speed as you approach. The work is on or past the shoulder rather than in your lane, and the guide still asks you to slow down as you approach it. A lane closure asks more. For a lane closure, merge into the marked open lane and slow to the posted work zone speed limit. That is two actions, not one. You move over into the lane that is marked as open, and you bring your speed down to the posted work zone speed limit, which can be lower than the limit you were driving before the work zone began.

Here is a trap. Because both types start with orange signs and slowing, learners often treat them as the same. A shoulder work zone asks you mainly to slow down, while a lane closure also asks you to merge into an open lane and drop to the work zone speed limit. If a question describes work on or past the shoulder, the answer is to reduce speed as you approach. If it describes a closed lane, the answer includes merging into the marked open lane as well as slowing to the posted work zone speed limit. An answer that only says slow down is incomplete for a lane closure, because the merge is part of what the guide asks.

lines.text: One lane of a two-lane road closed.
A fixed site on the road.

narration.text: A flagging operation closes one lane of a two-lane, two-way road, with flaggers at each end. Picture an ordinary road with one lane in each direction. When one of those lanes is closed for work, the flaggers at each end direct the traffic. Your job is to be ready to stop and follow their directions. The guide describes a flagging operation as a fixed site on a two-lane road with flaggers at both ends, so the work stays in one place while traffic is directed past it. When you see a flagger, approach ready to stop where the flagger directs you, and move on only when the flagger's directions tell you to go.

lines.text: Work vehicles move along a travel lane.
Protective vehicle with flashing arrow panel.

narration.text: A mobile work zone is different because it moves. In a mobile work zone, slow or stopped work vehicles move along a travel lane, and workers may step out, so expect them near the road. As you approach, look for a protective vehicle in the lane with a flashing arrow panel showing which lane to merge into. It is often signed Slow Vehicles. Follow the direction shown on the flashing arrow panel, and watch for several slow or stopped work vehicles, not just one. The protective vehicle is your first clue to the zone, and the arrow panel tells you which lane to use. Beyond it, expect workers stepping out and more work vehicles along the lane.

lines.text: Flagging: fixed site, flaggers both ends.
Mobile: moves behind a protective vehicle.

narration.text: Here is the second trap in this lesson. A flagging operation is a fixed site on a two-lane road with flaggers at both ends, while a mobile work zone moves along a travel lane behind a protective vehicle with an arrow panel. The clues are different people and different devices. Flaggers standing at each end of a closed lane point to a flagging operation, and there you are ready to stop and follow their directions. A protective vehicle with a flashing arrow panel, often signed Slow Vehicles, points to a mobile work zone, and there you follow the arrow panel's direction and watch for several slow or stopped work vehicles.

lines.text: Ivy sees a slow truck in her lane.
It has a flashing arrow panel.
Work vehicles move ahead of it.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ivy comes over a rise and sees a slow truck in her lane with a flashing arrow panel and a Slow Vehicles sign. Ahead of it, work vehicles are moving slowly along the same lane. What kind of work zone is this, and what should Ivy do? Work it out before reading on. This is a mobile work zone, and the truck is the protective vehicle. Ivy follows the direction shown on the flashing arrow panel and merges into the lane it shows. She watches for several slow or stopped work vehicles and expects workers to step out near the road. It is not a flagging operation, which is a fixed site with flaggers at both ends.

title.text: Match the zone, match the move

narration.text: To close, match each work zone with its move. For a shoulder work zone, where the work is on or past the shoulder, reduce speed as you approach. For a lane closure, merge into the marked open lane and slow to the posted work zone speed limit. For a flagging operation, which closes one lane of a two-lane, two-way road with flaggers at each end, be ready to stop and follow their directions. For a mobile work zone, look for the protective vehicle with a flashing arrow panel, follow the direction it shows, and watch for several slow or stopped work vehicles and for workers who may step out. Next we leave work zones for guide, service and route signs.

why_how.text: Sign colors tell you whether a sign guides you to a place or points to a service.
Route shapes and numbers, exit numbers and reference markers tell you what road you are on, which way it runs and where you are.

scenario.text: Kai is driving west on an east-west interstate and wonders whether the exit numbers will go up or down.

reasoning.text: Exit numbers on east-west interstates start at zero in the west and rise heading east.

result.text: Driving west, Kai will see the exit numbers get smaller.

claim.text: Common mistake: reading a three-digit interstate's first digit as a direction, the way odd and even route numbers work.

correction.text: Three-digit interstate numbers split by first digit: even means a loop around a city, odd means a spur into it.

memory_support.text: Green or brown guides, blue serves; even loops, odd spurs.

prompt.text: Kai is driving west on an east-west interstate. Will the next exits carry larger or smaller numbers?

answer.text: Smaller. Exit numbers start at zero in the west and rise heading east, so driving west they get smaller.

rationale.text: Driving west on an east-west interstate, exit numbers get smaller, and driving south on a north-south interstate, they also get smaller.

narration.text: This lesson covers the signs that help you find your way. Guide signs are green or brown squares or rectangles with white letters, showing direction and distance to places. Service signs are blue squares or rectangles with white letters or symbols, marking services such as rest areas and hospitals. Then come route signs, whose shape tells you the road type and whose number tells you which way the route runs. We will decode three-digit interstate numbers, see how exit numbers rise along an interstate, and finish with the emergency reference markers along the outside shoulder. The guide's advice is to plan a trip with a highway map and follow the route signs along the way.

lines.text: Guide signs: green or brown, white letters.
Service signs: blue, white letters or symbols.

narration.text: Color tells you what kind of help a sign offers. Guide signs are green or brown squares or rectangles with white letters. They show direction and distance to cities, airports and state lines, or to parks, historic sites and museums. Service signs are blue squares or rectangles with white letters or symbols, and they mark services such as rest areas and hospitals. Put simply, guide signs are green or brown with white lettering, while service signs are blue with white letters or symbols. The guide also pictures an Authorized Safety Inspection Station sign among the guide and service signs. When you need a place, look for green or brown; when you need a service, look for blue.

lines.text: Interstate, United States, state or county.

narration.text: Route signs carry two kinds of information. The shape of a route sign tells you the road type, whether interstate, United States, state or county. The number tells you the direction. Routes running north and south carry odd numbers, and routes running east and west carry even numbers. So a single glance at a route sign answers two questions: what kind of road this is, from the shape, and which way it runs, from whether the number is odd or even. The guide's travel advice builds on this. Plan a trip with a highway map and follow the route signs along the way so you do not get lost, checking the shape and the number on each sign you pass.

lines.text: Even first digit: loop around a city.
Odd first digit: spur into a city.

narration.text: Three-digit interstate numbers add one more layer. A three-digit interstate number starting with an even digit, such as I-two hundred seventy or I-four hundred thirty-five, loops around a city. One starting with an odd digit, such as I-one hundred fifty-five or I-one hundred seventy, is a spur into a city. Only the first digit decides this. Even means a loop around a city, odd means a spur into it. So when you see a three-digit interstate, look at its first digit before anything else. An even first digit tells you the road loops around a city, and an odd first digit tells you it is a spur heading into one.

lines.text: Route number odd or even: direction.
Three-digit first digit: loop or spur.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from two rules that both use odd and even. For route numbers, routes running north and south carry odd numbers, and routes running east and west carry even numbers. For three-digit interstate numbers, the first digit splits them: even means a loop around a city, odd means a spur into it. Learners often blend the two and decide that an even first digit means east and west, or that an odd one means north and south. Keep them apart. When a question is about which way a route runs, use the odd and even route number rule. When it asks whether a three-digit interstate loops around a city or spurs into it, look only at the first digit.

lines.text: East-west: zero in the west, rising east.
North-south: start in the south, rising north.
Markers every two-tenths of a mile.

narration.text: Exit numbers follow a pattern too. On east-west interstates they start at zero in the west and rise heading east, and on north-south interstates they start in the south and rise heading north. Turn that around and you get the other half: driving west on an east-west interstate, exit numbers get smaller, and driving south on a north-south interstate, they also get smaller. Along the outside shoulder you will also see emergency reference markers. They mark the road edge and show direction and route number, and they are spaced every two-tenths of a mile so one is always in view, showing your direction and route wherever you are.

lines.text: Kai drives west on an interstate.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Kai is driving west on an east-west interstate. He has just passed an exit and wonders whether the next exits will carry larger or smaller numbers. Which is it? Work it out before reading on. The numbers get smaller. Exit numbers on east-west interstates start at zero in the west and rise heading east. Kai is heading west, toward the end where the numbers start, so each exit he reaches will carry a smaller number. The same idea works on north-south interstates. Numbers start in the south and rise heading north, so driving south on a north-south interstate, the exit numbers also get smaller.

lines.text: Green or brown guides; blue serves.
Shape: road type. Odd or even: direction.
Exits rise heading east and north.

narration.text: To close, pull the wayfinding rules together. Guide signs are green or brown with white lettering, and service signs are blue with white letters or symbols. A route sign's shape tells you the road type, whether interstate, United States, state or county, and its number tells direction: odd for north and south, even for east and west. A three-digit interstate starting with an even digit loops around a city, and one starting with an odd digit is a spur into a city. Exit numbers rise heading east or north, and emergency reference markers every two-tenths of a mile keep one always in view. Plan with a highway map and follow the route signs.
